label: re:duality
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{re:duality}\rm
To place the definition of the \(L\log L\)-Luxemburg discrepancy in a broader context, we briefly explain its connection to numerical integration. The associate norm of the Luxemburg norm $\|\cdot\|_{\Phi}$ is defined as 
\begin{equation}\label{def:assoc:norm}
\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{\Phi,*} :=\sup_{\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\Phi} \le1} \int_{[0,1]^d} |f(\boldsymbol{t})g(\boldsymbol{t})|\,\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{t}.
\end{equation}     
Let $\mathcal{F}_d$ be the anchored Sobolev--Orlicz space consisting of all functions $h$ on $[0,1]^d$ for which there exists a measurable function $g$ with $\|g\|_{\Phi,\ast}<\infty$ such that
\[
h(\boldsymbol{x})=\int_{[\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{x}]}g(\boldsymbol{t})\,\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{t}.
\]
Write $Dh:=g$, which is uniquely determined almost everywhere, and equip this space with the norm $\|h\|_{\mathcal{F}_d}:=\|Dh\|_{\Phi,\ast}$.

For integration in $\mathcal{F}_d$ let $I(f) = \int_{[0,1]^d} f(\boldsymbol{t}) \,\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{t}$, and use $\mathcal{A}$-weighted linear rules $Q_{\mathcal{P},\mathcal{A}}(f)=\sum_{k=1}^N a_k f(\boldsymbol{x}_k)$, where $\mathcal{P}=\{\boldsymbol{x}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{x}_N\}$ and $\mathcal{A}=\{a_1,\ldots,a_N\}$ are as before. The worst-case error of such rules $Q_{\mathcal{P},\mathcal{A}}$ for integration in $\mathcal{F}_d$ is defined as $$e(Q_{\mathcal{P},\mathcal{A}};\mathcal{F}_d):=\sup_{\substack{f \in \mathcal{F}_d\\ \|f\|_{\mathcal{F}_d} \le 1}}|I(f)-Q_{\mathcal{P},\mathcal{A}}(f)|.$$ Then we have the ``discrepancy-integration duality'' 
\begin{equation}\label{disc:int:dual}
  e(Q_{\mathcal{P},\mathcal{A}};\mathcal{F}_d)=D_N^{\Phi}(\overline{\mathcal{P}},\mathcal{A}),
\end{equation}
where $\overline{\mathcal{P}}:=\{\boldsymbol{1}-\boldsymbol{x} : \boldsymbol{x} \in \mathcal{P}\}$. For the initial error $e(0;\mathcal{F}_d):= \sup_{\|f\|_{\mathcal{F}_d}\le 1} |I(f)|$ we have $e(0;\mathcal{F}_d)=\|v_d\|_{\Phi}=\operatorname{disc}_{\Phi}(0,d)$. The proof of the discrepancy-integration duality is given in the Appendix.

label: lem:modular
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The function \(\Phi\) is continuous and strictly increasing on \([0,\infty)\).  Hence, for every point at which \(|f|>0\), the quantity
\(\Phi(|f|/K)\) is strictly decreasing in \(K\).  Since \(f\) is bounded, dominated convergence shows that \(K\mapsto\rho_\Phi(f/K)\) is continuous on every compact subinterval of \((0,\infty)\).  The limit as \(K\to\infty\) is zero by dominated convergence.  Since \(f\) is not zero almost everywhere, there are numbers \(c>0\) and \(m>0\) such that the set \(\{|f|\geq c\}\) has measure at least \(m\).  Therefore
\[
 \rho_\Phi(f/K)\geq m\Phi(c/K)\rightarrow\infty
 \qquad \mbox{as } K\downarrow 0.
\]
Thus there is a unique \(K_0>0\) for which \(\rho_\Phi(f/K_0)=1\).  By the definition of the Luxemburg norm, this \(K_0\) equals \(\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\Phi}\).  The last assertion follows from monotonicity.
head: environment

label: lem:L1-embedding
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:L1-embedding}
For every measurable \(f\) on \([0,1]^d\) we have $\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{L_1}\leq\kappa\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\Phi}$.
head: environment
name: Embedding into \(L_1\

title: Proof
body_md:
The assertion is trivial if \(f=0\) almost everywhere or \(\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\Phi}=\infty\). Otherwise, let \(K>\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\Phi}\). By the definition of the infimum, there exists \(K_0<K\) such that \(\rho_\Phi(f/K_0)\leq1\); hence monotonicity gives
\[
 \int_{[0,1]^d}\Phi\!\left(\frac{|f(\boldsymbol{t})|}{K}\right) \,\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{t}\leq1.
\]
Since the unit cube has Lebesgue measure one and \(\Phi\) is convex, Jensen's inequality gives
\[
 \Phi\!\left(\frac{\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{L_1}}{K}\right)
 \leq\int_{[0,1]^d}\Phi\!\left(\frac{|f(\boldsymbol{t})|}{K}\right) \,\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{t}
 \leq 1=\Phi(\kappa).
\]
The function \(\Phi\) is increasing, so \(\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{L_1}\leq\kappa K\).  Letting \(K\downarrow\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\Phi}\) proves Lemma~\ref{lem:L1-embedding}.

body_md:
\label{re:1}\rm
For every $p>1$ there exists a $C_p>0$ with the following property: for every measurable \(f\) on \([0,1]^d\) we have $\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\Phi}\leq C_p \left\lVert f\right\rVert_{L_p}$. The proof is given in the Appendix.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(S_d\) be as in \eqref{eq:Sd} and define $A_{d,\delta} :=\{S_d\leq (\frac12+\delta)d\}$. We first estimate the probability of its complement.  If \(Y\) is exponential with rate two, then, for \(\lambda \in (0,2)\),
\[
 \mathbb{E}[{\rm e}^{\lambda Y}]=\frac{2}{2-\lambda}.
\]
Therefore, by the exponential Markov inequality, 
\[
 \nu_d\left(S_d\geq (\tfrac12+\delta)d\right)
 \leq {\rm e}^{-\lambda (1/2+\delta) d}\, \left(\frac{2}{2-\lambda}\right)^d.
\]
Choosing $\lambda=2-(1/2+\delta)^{-1}=\frac{4\delta}{1+2\delta}\in(0,2)$ yields
\begin{align*}
 \nu_d(A_{d,\delta}^c)
 &\leq {\rm e}^{-d (2\delta-\log(1+2\delta))} ={\rm e}^{-I_\delta d}.
\end{align*}
The number \(I_\delta\) is positive because
\(x-\log(1+x)>0\) for every \(x>0\).

On \(A_{d,\delta}\),
\[
 v_d(\boldsymbol T)={\rm e}^{-S_d}
 \geq {\rm e}^{-(1/2+\delta)d}.
\]
Since \(\left\lVert v_d\right\rVert_{\Phi}=\alpha_d2^{-d}\), it follows that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:volume-ratio-lower}
 \frac{v_d(\boldsymbol T)}{\varepsilon \left\lVert v_d\right\rVert_{\Phi}}
 \geq\frac{{\rm e}^{(\log2-1/2-\delta)d}}{\varepsilon \alpha_d}
 =\frac{{\rm e}^{(c_0-\delta)d}}{\varepsilon \alpha_d}
 \qquad\text{on }A_{d,\delta}.
\end{equation}
For every \(x\geq0\), \eqref{eq:volume-ratio-lower} implies, pointwise on
\(A_{d,\delta}\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pointwise-localization}
 x
 \leq\tau+
 \frac{x\log\!\left(1+\frac{v_d(\boldsymbol T)}{\varepsilon \left\lVert v_d\right\rVert_{\Phi}}x\right)}{L_d}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, if \(x<\tau\), then the right-hand side is at least \(\tau>x\).  If \(x\geq\tau\), then
\[
 \log\!\left(1+\frac{v_d(\boldsymbol T)}{\varepsilon \left\lVert v_d\right\rVert_{\Phi}}x\right)
 \geq\log\!\left(1+\frac{\tau {\rm e}^{(c_0-\delta)d}}{\varepsilon \alpha_d}\right)
 =L_d,
\]
so the second term on the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:pointwise-localization} is at least \(x\).

Apply \eqref{eq:pointwise-localization} with \(x=X\), multiply by
\(\mathbf{1}_{A_{d,\delta}}\), take expectations, and use
\eqref{eq:modular-X}.  We obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:localized-X}
\mathbb{E}_{\nu_d}[X\mathbf{1}_{A_{d,\delta}}] \leq\tau+\frac{\varepsilon \alpha_d}{L_d}.
\end{equation}

For \(z\geq0\) we have $z^{1/2}\geq1-|z-1|$. Indeed, for \(0\leq z\leq1\), the right-hand side equals
\(z \le z^{1/2}\); for $z \ge 1$ it equals \(2-z\leq1\leq z^{1/2}\).  Applying our estimate to \(Z\) on \(A_{d,\delta}\) gives
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}_{\nu_d}[Z^{1/2}] &\geq\mathbb{E}_{\nu_d}[Z^{1/2}\mathbf{1}_{A_{d,\delta}}] \geq\nu_d(A_{d,\delta}) -\mathbb{E}_{\nu_d}[X\mathbf{1}_{A_{d,\delta}}].
\end{align*}
The probability estimate and \eqref{eq:localized-X} prove
\eqref{eq:moment-lower-explicit}.

It remains to show that the right-hand side of
\eqref{eq:moment-lower-explicit} is eventually positive.  By
\eqref{eq:ad-asymptotic}, \(\lim_{d \rightarrow \infty} \alpha_d/d = c_0\) and by \eqref{eq:logad}, \(\lim_{d \rightarrow \infty} \log \alpha_d/d = 0\).  Writing
\[
 L_d=\log(1+{\rm e}^{q_d}) \qquad \mbox{ and } \qquad 
 q_d=(c_0-\delta)d-\log \alpha_d+\log(\tau/\varepsilon),
\]
we have \(\lim_{d \rightarrow \infty} q_d/d = c_0-\delta>0\), and hence $\lim_{d \rightarrow \infty} L_d/d = c_0-\delta$. Therefore,
\begin{equation*}                    
 \lim_{d \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\varepsilon \alpha_d}{L_d} = \frac{\varepsilon c_0}{c_0-\delta}.
\end{equation*}
By \eqref{eq:delta-tau},
\[
 b_\infty
 :=1-\tau-\frac{\varepsilon c_0}{c_0-\delta}>0.
\]
The right-hand side of \eqref{eq:moment-lower-explicit} converges to
\(b_\infty\).  Thus it is at least, for example,
\(b=b_\infty/2>0\) for all sufficiently large \(d\), proving
\eqref{eq:moment-lower}.
